page2_img_1.png.title: DVC history diagram showing a branch and its merge
page2_img_1.png.description: A schematic of a distributed version control (DVC) history showing the mainline (top row of circles) and a feature branch labeled "my-branch" (bottom row). Circles represent commits; solid arrows indicate the temporal order of commits along each line, and dashed arrows mark the branch-off and later merge relationships between the branch and the mainline. The diagram conveys that DVC records these parent/merge relationships (the dashed edges are treated like regular commit edges), in contrast to older centralized VCs where such cross-branch relationships could be untracked.

page8_img_1.png.title: Monte Carlo tiling of observed branch lengths onto linearized history D
page8_img_1.png.description: Three-panel diagram illustrating the Monte Carlo construction: left, an observed DVC fragment with a green mainline segment (4 commits) and two feature branches (blue: 3 commits; red: 2 commits). The middle panel shows the extracted multiset of branch lengths (4, 2, 3). The right panel depicts these length segments randomly projected (tiled) onto the linearized timeline D as colored horizontal segments labeled with their lengths, with curved arrows mapping each original branch-length element to its placement on D. This tiling is repeated (1000 simulations) to create simulated branches of the same length distribution as a baseline for comparing observed branch cohesion against random sequences drawn from D.

page6_img_1.png.title: Branched vs. Linearized Commit History (projection onto D)
page6_img_1.png.description: The diagram contrasts a branched DVC history (top) with its linearized projection D (bottom). In the branched view two parallel lines show commits 1→3 and 2→4 that converge at an explicit merge commit M and then continue to commit 5; in the linearized view the same commits are simply ordered 1–2–3–4–5 and the merge node M is omitted. The figure demonstrates how projecting branch histories onto a single timeline makes concurrent, intervening commits explicit (those between a branch ancestor a and a descendant c) and is used in the paper to overapproximate potential integration interruptions.

page8_img_2.png.title: Distribution of Linux branch lengths (log scale)
page8_img_2.png.description: A boxplot (y-axis on a log scale) showing the distribution of observed branch lengths in the Linux kernel history. The median branch length is about 6–7 commits with an interquartile range roughly from ~4 to ~12 commits and a minimum of 2 commits, but the distribution is strongly positively skewed with many extreme outliers extending to very large lengths. As noted in the paper, 90% of branches are shorter than 35 commits (branches longer than 35 commits are rare—fewer than 25 instances—which is why subsequent analyses were truncated at 35). This figure visually motivates the heavy-tailed nature of branch durations used in the Monte Carlo simulations.

page11_img_1.png.title: Linearized history, intervening files, and distraction index
page11_img_1.png.description: The diagram shows a linearized commit timeline D (a horizontal line with small ovals for commits) and highlights a specific commit c and its nearest non-merge ancestor a, with the intervening sequence D(a,c) marked between them. Above each commit are stacked colored rectangles representing the files modified by that commit; the union of files changed in the intervening commits is drawn as the set Fi (purple), while the files changed by c are drawn as fm(c) (green). A Venn-style overlap Fi ∩ fm(c) is emphasized to represent files modified both in the intervening history and in c, and the right-hand pictorial shows that the index of similarity δ is the ratio |Fi ∩ fm(c)| / |fm(c)| used to classify c as “distracted.” The figure therefore visualizes the formal definitions from the text for intervening files and distraction, and how overlap of changesets quantifies potential integration interruptions.

page12_img_1.png.title: Distracted commits vs. index of similarity in Linux linearized history
page12_img_1.png.description: A line plot showing how the fraction of commits that are “distracted” falls as the index of similarity δ (the fraction of a commit’s files that also changed in intervening commits) increases from 0 to 1. At δ = 0 (any intervening files present) there is a large spike (~30%), but when requiring even a small overlap (δ = 0.1) the distracted-commit rate drops to about 4.5% (95% CI 4.47%–4.69%). The curve then declines gradually to ≈2.8% at δ = 1.0 (complete overlap; 95% CI 2.47%–2.93%), indicating that non-empty intersections occur roughly once every 22 commits and full overlaps roughly once every 35 commits. This demonstrates that although intervening changes are common, substantially overlapping (potentially distracting) concurrent edits are relatively rare.

page8_img_3.png.title: Mean Directory Distance by Branch Length: Observed vs Simulated Cohesion
page8_img_3.png.description: The plot shows mean directory distance (y-axis) for branches of different lengths (x-axis, 1–35), comparing observed Linux branch means (black diamonds) to simulated branch means over the linearized history (black dots) with 95% confidence intervals (vertical lines and open circles). For almost every branch length the observed Linux means lie below the simulation means, indicating observed branches are significantly more cohesive (smaller directory distance); significance is indicated by black diamonds (p < 0.05) and a red square marks the single non-significant point at length 34. The cohesion advantage grows with branch length — about 0.12 directories at length 2 and roughly 1.5 directories at length 32 — and the authors report a Spearman correlation r = 0.69 (p << .001) between branch length and the cohesion difference. The simulations are based on 1,000 random tilings of the linearized history D and the plot is truncated at 35 commits because longer branches were too rare for reliable estimates.
